title: Sunflower conjecture
formal:
For every integer \(r\ge3\), does there exist a real constant \(C_r\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite set \(X\), and every family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\{S\subseteq X:|S|=k\}\),
\[
|\mathcal F|>C_r^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\text{ distinct }S_1,\ldots,S_r\in\mathcal F\ \exists K\subseteq X\ \forall i\ne j:\ S_i\cap S_j=K?
\]
The constant may depend on \(r\) but not on the set size \(k\), the ground set or the family. The conclusion is the existence of an ordinary \(r\)-sunflower.
definitions:
A family here is a finite set of subsets, so identical members are not repeated. It is \(k\)-uniform when every member has exactly \(k\) elements. There is no bound on the finite ground-set size \(|X|\). An \(r\)-sunflower consists of \(r\) pairwise distinct members whose pairwise intersections are all the same set \(K\), called the core. For \(r\ge3\), this core also equals the intersection of all selected members. Removing \(K\) leaves pairwise disjoint petals. The core may be empty, in which case the selected sets are pairwise disjoint. For distinct equal-sized members their petals are nonempty.

The quantifier order is \(\forall r\,\exists C_r\,\forall k,X,\mathcal F\). No single base independent of \(r\) is requested. One may equivalently require an integer \(C_r\ge2\), since a larger integer base preserves the upper bound. An eventual bound for all sufficiently large \(k\), with the threshold depending on \(r\), also yields the displayed all-\(k\) formulation by enlarging \(C_r\) to cover finitely many small sizes.

The classical sunflower lemma bounds the size of any sunflower-free \(k\)-uniform family by \(k!(r-1)^k\), independently of its ground set. Consequently the largest such size \(S_r(k)\) exists as a finite integer, even though the ground set is unrestricted. The conjecture is equivalently \(S_r(k)\le C_r^k\) for all \(k\). It does not ask for the exact value, a numerical estimate or constant-factor asymptotics of \(S_r(k)\).

The source also states the conjecture for sets of size at most \(k\). Padding every smaller set to size \(k\) with fresh elements unique to that member preserves pairwise intersections and reduces that variant to the displayed one. This observation is not a claim about robust sunflowers: their probabilistic coverage requirement is stronger, and lower bounds for that stronger structure do not refute the ordinary conjecture.

There is no computational requirement on finding the sunflower or computing the constants. This is a quantified extremal-combinatorial proposition, so the numerical absolute-error convention does not replace it.

context_blocks.text: The classical lemma forces a sunflower only after a factorial-sized threshold. The conjecture would replace this by an exponential whose base is independent of the set size.

Modern bounds remove most of the classical growth but still have a base growing logarithmically with the set size. The robust sunflower method has its own obstruction at that scale, which does not settle ordinary sunflowers.
Sunflower structure supports computational lower bounds and other combinatorial reductions. A uniform exponential threshold would strengthen the general principle used in such applications.

why: A general combinatorial principle with established applications to computational lower bounds and parameterized reductions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed conjecture or its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite base for every fixed \(r\ge3\). A negative proof must supply one fixed \(r\ge3\) for which every candidate base \(C\ge1\) admits a \(k\)-uniform family of more than \(C^k\) members with no \(r\)-sunflower. Improving known superconstant bases, proving only the case of one petal count, or disproving a robust-sunflower variant does not decide the full statement.

progress.text: The primary breakthrough gives bounds with a base polylogarithmic in the uniformity, improving the classical factorial threshold while retaining Conjecture 1.3.

Rao’s journal survey, in the checked September 2025 author manuscript, states the conjecture as open and surveys an \(O(r\log k)^k\) bound. It distinguishes the necessary logarithmic dependence for robust sunflowers from the ordinary target.

sentences: A sunflower is a collection of distinct sets with one common pairwise intersection.
The conjecture fixes the number of petals and asks how many equal-sized sets force that structure.
It asks for an exponential threshold whose base depends only on the petal count.
The ground set is any finite set, and the core may be empty.
Known logarithmic-base bounds and limitations for robust sunflowers leave the ordinary exponential conjecture open in the checked sources.

formulation_history.formal: For each fixed integer \(r\ge 3\), determine, up to constant factors as \(k\to \infty , S_{r}(k)\): the largest number of distinct k-element sets in a family containing no r members whose pairwise intersections are all equal, where the finite ground set is unrestricted.
formulation_history.answer_criterion: Give functions \(f_{r}(k)\) and, for every fixed integer \(r\ge 3\), constants \(0<c_{r}\le C_{r}<\infty\) with \(c_{r} f_{r}(k)\le S_{r}(k)\le C_{r} f_{r}(k)\) for every \(k\ge 1\), absorbing finitely many small k into the constants if needed. Prove both a universal upper bound and existence of matching sunflower-free families in Lean. An exponential upper bound by itself does not determine the growth within constant factors.
